Peaucellier-Lipkin Linkage

GeometryCirclesInvariants
Game: Move the rings of a seven-rod machine and watch one dot draw a straight line; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag O, A, B, C or P, or focus a ring and press the arrow keys. Drag A around the dashed circle to draw the line, and use the boxes and buttons to change the picture.

Drag a dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps). Drag A along the dashed circle to make C draw the green line.

Look for the math

Seven rods turn a circle into a straight line. There is no motor and no hidden track: one product of two distances simply refuses to change as the rods move.

The product that never changes

The four short rods make a rhombus ABCD of side s. The two long rods from O to B and D have length L. Let M be the crossing point of the rhombus's two diagonals. Because MB² + OM² = L² and MB² + MA² = s², subtracting gives OM² − MA² = L² − s². Since A and C sit opposite each other around M, the page's identity follows:

OA · OC = (OM − MA)(OM + MA) = OM² − MA² = OB² − AB²

With the applet's rods L = 80 and s = 30, this product is always 80² − 30² = 5500. The logic test confirmed it on 697 reachable positions drawn from 1,440 tried rod set-ups: the largest error was below 10−6.

Points paired by a circle

The equation above says exactly that A and C are paired by circle inversion in O with power k = L² − s²: each lies on the same ray from O, and the product of their distances from O is k. The rods enforce both conditions at once, so they behave like a mechanical inverter. On the test's 1,440 set-ups, all four rhombus sides equalled s, both long rods equalled L, M was the shared midpoint of AC and BD, and A, C stayed on one ray from O.

Why C draws a line

The extra rod PA has the same length as OP, so A is held on a circle centred at P that passes straight through O. Inversion sends a circle through its centre to a straight line: if u is the unit vector from O to P, every image C satisfies u · (C − F) = 0, where F = O + k·u/(2·OP). That line is at right angles to OP. The test swept A through 720 positions around the circle: 334 gave a reachable linkage, and every one of those C's lay on the same line to within 10−6. C covers only a finite segment, as the page says.

What the applet really does

The page warns that an analog device cannot be perfect and that rounding errors appear when the drawing point races off towards infinity. This port keeps that behaviour: it uses the applet's own guards (OA ≥ 0.1, a positive rhombus half-diagonal, and |x|, |y| ≤ 2000 for C) and does not smooth away the wobble. The check script transcribes the original FindPeauc and all five drag methods a second time and compares them on 1,995 pointer targets: no difference above 10−8. The Java panel's mouse rings become focusable SVG handles, and Reset, Clear line and the two boxes are new browser controls; the geometry underneath them is unchanged. The page still embeds the original Java applet, which browsers no longer run.

Try dragging A slowly around the dashed circle: watch the reading in the status line stay at 5500 while C paints a straight line. Then drag A towards O and see where the linkage refuses to close.
